– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The test `testCalendarTimezoneRespected()` shows that when formatting a Calendar object with a specific time zone using FastDateFormat, the "z" pattern (which represents the time zone) prints the default machine's time zone name rather than the Calendar's time zone name. The test first sets up a Calendar in a non-default time zone, uses SimpleDateFormat set to that time zone to get the expected formatted string, and then compares it to the string from FastDateFormat formatting. The failure shows the time zone format in FastDateFormat does not respect the Calendar's time zone, even though the time component itself respects the Calendar's time zone.

Looking into the FastDateFormat class, we find that the `format(Calendar)` method simply delegates to `printer.format(Calendar)`. The printer is an instance of FastDatePrinter, which is responsible for the actual formatting work. The FastDatePrinter's `format(Calendar)` method calls `format(Calendar, StringBuffer)` and returns the formatted String. The latter calls `applyRules(Calendar, StringBuffer)` to perform the formatting.

The core issue stems from the way FastDatePrinter formats the "z" time zone pattern. Instead of using the Calendar's time zone, it uses the time zone stored internally in FastDatePrinter (likely the default system time zone unless explicitly set). Thus, time is formatted with respect to the Calendar's zone (because the calendar's time is used), but the zone name displayed (the "z" pattern) is incorrectly taken from the FastDatePrinter's zone, ignoring the Calendar's own zone setting.

This explains the bug report's assertion that "FastDateFormat's 'z' pattern does not respect timezone of Calendar instances passed to format()" and why the test fails by showing the default time zone name instead of the Calendar's zone name.

Recent reports are unrelated; this is a timezone formatting mismatch issue due to FastDatePrinter's handling (or mishandling) of the time zone when formatting Calendar objects.

The bug occurs because FastDatePrinter caches or uses a fixed time zone (set at construction) for zone-formatting, rather than adapting to the time zone of the Calendar instance passed for formatting. This leads to inconsistent timezone display when formatting Calendars with non-default zones.

Suggested inspection and fix should be in FastDatePrinter.format(Calendar), especially the applyRules() method and how the "z" pattern is resolved to a zone name string, ensuring it retrieves time zone info from the Calendar's time zone rather than using a fixed internal time zone.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
